title: 22. Interview: Blue-Green Deployment
summary: Interview Q&A for Blue-Green Deployment — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Blue-Green Deployment interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is blue-green deployment, and what problem does it solve that in-place upgrades do not?
**Answer:** Blue-green deployment runs two identical production environments — "blue" (current live) and "green" (new staged) — and switches traffic between them via a single router update, making the cutover instant and fully reversible. In-place upgrades stop the old version, install the new, restart, and hope nothing breaks; if it does, you are down until you reverse the upgrade, and reverse upgrades are notoriously unreliable (databases rarely downgrade cleanly, configuration drift accumulates). Blue-green eliminates this class of risk: the new version is fully deployed and smoke-tested before it receives any traffic, the cutover is one router change taking seconds, and rollback is the same router change reversed. The cost is roughly 2× infrastructure during the cutover window (both environments running simultaneously). The benefit is zero-downtime, reversible releases even for major version changes — which is why Netflix (red/black on Spinnaker), Amazon, and Google use it as the default release strategy. For teams that release frequently or where downtime is costly, blue-green is the standard; for rare releases with generous maintenance windows, simpler strategies may suffice.

**Visual:**
```
   in-place upgrade (risky):
   stop v1.5 -> install v1.6 -> start v1.6 -> hope
   if v1.6 broken: stop v1.6 -> install v1.5 -> start v1.5 (may not work)
   downtime = upgrade time + rollback time if needed

   blue-green (safe):
   deploy v1.6 to green (zero traffic), smoke test
   router: 100% blue -> 100% green   (~5 seconds, reversible)
   if green broken: router: 100% green -> 100% blue  (~5 seconds)
   downtime = 0 (cutover is instant)
   cost = 2x infra during cutover window
```

### Q2. How do you handle database schema changes in a blue-green deployment?
**Answer:** The challenge is that blue and green share one database (you cannot duplicate it without divergence), so both versions must work against the same schema during the cutover window. The pattern is "expand-and-contract": first deploy a version that supports both the old and new schema (the expand step) — green's code reads the old columns and writes both old and new; then run the schema migration (adding the new column, populating it from the old); then deploy a future version that uses only the new schema and drops the old (the contract step). For example, renaming a column: expand by adding the new column alongside the old and writing to both; migrate by backfilling the new from the old; contract by dropping the old column in a future release. For breaking changes that cannot be made backward-compatible (changing a column type), the pattern is "shadow writes" — green writes to a new table while blue continues to write to the old, a backfill job copies between them, and cutover happens only when both are in sync. The cost is significant engineering discipline (multiple releases for each schema change); the benefit is zero-downtime, reversible releases even for stateful services.

**Visual:**
```
   expand-and-contract pattern:
   release 1 (blue v1.5):  uses old schema
   release 2 (green v1.6): supports both old + new schema (expand)
        -> migrate DB: add new column, backfill from old
   release 3 (blue v1.7):  uses only new schema (contract)
        -> migrate DB: drop old column

   example: rename column `name` -> `full_name`
   v1.5:  SELECT name FROM users
   v1.6:  SELECT full_name FROM users (expand: writes both name + full_name)
          migration: ALTER TABLE users ADD full_name; UPDATE users SET full_name=name
   v1.7:  SELECT full_name FROM users (contract: DROP COLUMN name)

   both blue + green work during the transition window -> zero-downtime
```

### Q3. What is canary analysis, and how does it combine with blue-green?
**Answer:** Canary analysis is the statistical comparison of the new version's metrics (error rate, latency, CPU, business KPIs) against the current version's, to decide whether the new version is healthy enough to receive more traffic. Pure blue-green shifts 100% of traffic in one cutover, which exposes all users to the new version simultaneously — if there is a subtle regression that only manifests under load, every user sees it. Canary within blue-green addresses this: after deploying green, shift 1% of traffic, watch metrics for 10 minutes, shift to 5%, watch, shift to 25%, watch, shift to 100%. At each stage, automated canary analysis (Netflix's Kayenta, Google's progressive rollout) compares green's metrics to blue's using statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U for distribution shifts, t-tests for mean changes) and produces a score: if green is statistically indistinguishable from blue, promote; if green is worse on any key metric, roll back automatically. The combination delivers blue-green's reversibility (the router can flip back instantly) with canary's gradual exposure (bugs are caught at 1% before they affect 100%). The trade-off is that canary analysis requires high-quality metrics and historical baselines to know what "statistically indistinguishable" means; for new services with sparse metrics, human judgment is still needed.

**Visual:**
```
   pure blue-green:       100% blue -> 100% green  (one shot, all users exposed)
   canary blue-green:     100% blue -> 1% green -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%
                            |         |        |        |
                          analyze   analyze  analyze  analyze
                          (statistical compare vs blue)
                          if FAIL at any stage -> rollback to 100% blue

   stages:
   T=0    0%  green, smoke test
   T=5m   1%  green, compare metrics (5m baseline)
   T=15m  5%  green, compare
   T=25m  25% green, compare
   T=35m  100% green, blue drained

   analysis: green err_rate vs blue err_rate (Mann-Whitney U)
             green p99 vs blue p99 (regression %)
             green business_KPI vs blue business_KPI
             score >= threshold -> promote; else rollback
```

### Q4. What is the cost of blue-green, and how do teams with large fleets or tight margins adapt?
**Answer:** Blue-green requires roughly 2× the production infrastructure during the cutover window — both blue and green are running simultaneously. If production is 100 instances, blue-green means 100 blue plus 100 green during the release, perhaps a few hours per week for weekly releases — roughly 5% additional monthly cost. For most teams this is acceptable. For teams with very large fleets (Netflix's thousands of instances per service) or tight margins (early-stage startups), the compromise is "rolling blue-green" — keep a small green environment (10% of production capacity) for canary validation, then either scale it up to 100% for the cutover (accepting brief 2× cost only at cutover moment) or accept a rolling in-place upgrade for the rest of the fleet after canary passes. Another adaptation is "blue-green on demand" — the green environment is provisioned only at release time via Infrastructure as Code and terminated immediately after cutover, so the 2× cost is incurred only for the duration of the release (minutes), not continuously. Spot instances can offset the cost further: blue runs on on-demand baseline, green runs on spot during the cutover window. The trade-off is operational complexity; the savings can be 50–80% of the nominal 2× cost.

**Visual:**
```
   pure blue-green:        blue 100% + green 100% = 2x cost (continuous)
   rolling blue-green:     blue 100% + green 10% canary = 1.1x cost
                             after canary: rolling upgrade blue 100%
                             cutover moment: brief 2x (seconds)
   blue-green on demand:   blue 100% (continuous)
                             at release: provision green 100%, cutover,
                             terminate green (cost only during release)
                             = ~5% additional monthly cost
   spot-assisted:          blue 100% on-demand + green 100% spot
                             = ~1.3x cost (spot ~30% of on-demand)

   teams with large fleets:
   Netflix, Amazon:  absorb full 2x (release hundreds of times/day, safety wins)
   startups:         rolling blue-green or on-demand green (cost-sensitive)
```

### Q5. Why is the router the "single source of truth," and what makes a good blue-green router?
**Answer:** The router — typically a load balancer (AWS ALB, NGINX, HAProxy) or a DNS record (Route 53 weighted policy) — is the only thing that decides which environment receives traffic, so the cutover and rollback are each a single configuration change. This is what makes blue-green instant and reversible: there is no gradual "drain blue, fill green" — there is one switch. A good blue-green router has four properties. First, atomic switching: the change from 100% blue to 100% green (or back) happens in one operation, not gradually, so there is no window of mixed traffic unless you explicitly want canary. Second, health-gated switching: the router only sends traffic to an environment that is healthy (passing health checks), so a half-booted green cannot receive traffic. Third, connection draining: when blue is removed from the router, in-flight requests on blue are allowed to complete (typically 30–300 seconds) before blue is terminated, so users do not see dropped connections. Fourth, fast propagation: the router's change must propagate to all clients quickly, which favors load balancers (instant, no DNS TTL) over DNS (limited by resolver caching). AWS ALB target group swaps take seconds; Route 53 weighted policy changes are bounded by TTL.

**Visual:**
```
   good router properties:
   1. atomic switch:    100% blue -> 100% green in one operation
                        (no mixed-traffic window unless canary wanted)
   2. health-gated:     router only sends to environments passing /health
                        (half-booted green cannot receive traffic)
   3. connection drain: in-flight requests on blue complete (30-300s)
                        before blue is terminated
   4. fast propagation: change reaches all clients quickly
                        ALB target group swap: ~5s
                        Route 53 weighted: bounded by TTL (60s+)

   router options:
   AWS ALB target group swap:   atomic, health-gated, ~5s   <- preferred
   NGINX upstream swap:         atomic, ~1s
   Route 53 weighted policy:    gradual, bounded by TTL
   Service mesh (Istio):        atomic, per-pod, ~1s
```

### Q6. What is the difference between blue-green and rolling deployment, and when do you choose each?
**Answer:** Blue-green runs two complete environments and switches traffic in one atomic operation; rolling deployment upgrades instances in place, a few at a time, until the whole fleet is on the new version. Blue-green's advantages are instant cutover, instant rollback (router flip), and full pre-deployment verification (green is tested before any traffic); its disadvantages are 2× infrastructure cost during cutover and the schema-migration complexity of a shared database. Rolling's advantages are low cost (no duplicate fleet) and simplicity (one environment, gradual replacement); its disadvantages are slow cutover (each batch takes minutes to verify), no instant rollback (you must redeploy the old version, which takes as long as the original rollout), and partial exposure to bugs (the first batch of users on the new version sees any bugs). Choose blue-green when releases are risky (major version changes, schema migrations), when downtime is unacceptable, or when the team releases frequently (the operational safety scales). Choose rolling for routine releases of stateless services where the cost of 2× infrastructure is not justified and the team accepts the slower rollback. Many teams use both: blue-green for high-risk releases, rolling for routine ones.

**Visual:**
```
   blue-green:                   rolling:
   blue 100% -> green 100%       batch 1 of 10 instances upgraded
   (one atomic switch)           batch 2 of 10
                                 ...
                                 batch 10 of 10 (all on new version)

   cutover:    instant (~5s)     slow (10 batches x 2min = 20min)
   rollback:   instant (~5s)     slow (redeploy old = 20min)
   cost:       2x during cutver  1x (no duplicate fleet)
   exposure:   full at cutover   gradual (batch 1 sees bugs first)
   schema:     needs expand-contract  simpler (one version at a time)

   use blue-green when:
   - risky release (major version, schema migration)
   - zero downtime required
   - frequent releases (safety scales)
   use rolling when:
   - routine stateless release
   - cost-sensitive
   - can tolerate slower rollback
```

### Q7. What is Netflix's red/black deployment on Spinnaker, and how does it automate blue-green?
**Answer:** Netflix's red/black deployment (their term for blue-green) on the Spinnaker platform automates the entire blue-green flow: a developer pushes code, Spinnaker deploys it to a new server group (the "red" candidate) with zero traffic, runs automated canary analysis comparing red's metrics to the current "black" live version's, and either promotes red to 100% traffic or rolls back automatically — the developer does not touch production. The key innovations are: first, automated canary analysis via Kayenta, which uses statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U, t-tests) to compare red's metrics to black's and produces a score; second, "managed delivery" pipelines that codify the release process as code, so every release follows the same safe steps; third, integration with their chaos engineering tools (Chaos Monkey, Chaos Kong) so releases are tested against simulated failures before promotion. The result is that Netflix releases hundreds of times per day with a release-failure rate below 1%, and most releases complete without human intervention. The trade-off is enormous engineering investment in Spinnaker, Kayenta, and the surrounding observability — justified for Netflix's scale, but a multi-year project for a smaller team to replicate. Smaller teams can adopt the same patterns using open-source tools: Argo Rollouts for Kubernetes, Flagger for progressive delivery, AWS CodeDeploy for blue-green on EC2/ECS.

**Visual:**
```
   Netflix red/black on Spinnaker:
   developer pushes code -> Spinnaker pipeline triggers
        |
   1. deploy to red server group (0% traffic)
        |
   2. smoke tests on red
        |
   3. canary 1% -> Kayenta analyzes red vs black (statistical)
        |       pass -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%
        |       fail -> auto rollback (delete red, black stays)
        |
   4. red promoted to 100%, black drained (kept warm 1h)
        |
   5. chaos test: Chaos Monkey kills red instances, verify auto-recovery
        |
   6. black terminated after 1h rollback window

   developer does not touch production; pipeline is fully automated
   Netflix: hundreds of releases/day, <1% failure rate

   open-source equivalents:
   Argo Rollouts (Kubernetes) | Flagger | AWS CodeDeploy
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your service has zero downtime tolerance, but your current deploy process is a rolling update that takes 20 minutes and occasionally fails mid-way. How do you move to blue-green?
**Answer:** I would migrate the service to blue-green in three phases. First, refactor for statelessness — ensure the service has no in-memory session state (move to Redis or external session store) so any instance can serve any request, and verify the database schema is forward/backward compatible (start using expand-and-contract for any new migrations). Second, set up the blue-green infrastructure: two identical target groups behind an AWS ALB (or two identical Kubernetes deployments behind a service), with the router pointing 100% at blue; the green environment is provisioned via the same Terraform module as blue but receives zero traffic. Third, build the deployment pipeline: deploy to green, run smoke tests against green's endpoints directly (bypassing the router), shift 1% traffic to green via a weighted target group, watch metrics for 10 minutes, shift to 5%/25%/100% progressively, and keep blue warm for a 1-hour rollback window before terminating. The migration is itself a blue-green deploy of the deployment process — start with one low-risk service, prove the pattern, then roll it out to others. The cost is 2× infrastructure during each release window (perhaps 5% additional monthly cost for weekly releases), offset by eliminating the 20-minute deploy window and the mid-deploy failures. The first release on blue-green is the riskiest; after that, the team has muscle memory and confidence.

**Visual:**
```
   phase 1: refactor for statelessness
     - move session state to Redis (any instance can serve any request)
     - adopt expand-and-contract for schema migrations
        |
   phase 2: set up blue-green infra
     ALB -> target group blue (100% traffic)   v1.5 live
        -> target group green (0% traffic)     v1.6 staged
     both provisioned via same Terraform module
        |
   phase 3: pipeline
     deploy green -> smoke test green (direct, bypass router)
     -> 1% canary -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%
     -> keep blue warm 1h, then terminate

   cost: 2x infra during release window (~5% monthly for weekly releases)
   benefit: zero-downtime, instant rollback, no mid-deploy failures
```

### Q2. You are deploying v2.0 of your service that renames the `users.email` column to `users.email_address`. How do you do this safely with blue-green?
**Answer:** A column rename is a breaking schema change that cannot be done in one release — v2.0 code expecting `email_address` would crash against the old schema, and v1.x code expecting `email` would crash against the new. The safe pattern is expand-and-contract across three releases. Release 1 (v1.x current): code uses `email`, schema has `email`. Release 2 (v1.x+1, "expand"): deploy code that reads from `email_address` if it exists, falls back to `email` otherwise, and writes to both columns; run the migration `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN email_address; UPDATE users SET email_address = email;` while both v1.x and v1.x+1 are running (blue and green share the database, both work against the new schema). Release 3 (v2.0, "contract"): deploy code that uses only `email_address`; after the cutover and a verification window, run `ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN email`. Each release is a standard blue-green deploy with instant rollback — if v1.x+1 has a bug, flip the router back to v1.x, which still works against the new schema because v1.x+1 wrote to both columns. The cost is two extra releases and a temporary duplicated column; the benefit is zero-downtime, reversible schema migration. Skipping the expand step (trying to do the rename in one release) would require downtime equal to the migration time and a non-reversible cutover.

**Visual:**
```
   release 1 (v1.x, current):
     code:  SELECT email FROM users
     schema: users(email, ...)

   release 2 (v1.x+1, EXPAND):
     code:  SELECT COALESCE(email_address, email) -- reads either
            INSERT ... email, email_address        -- writes both
     schema migration:
       ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN email_address VARCHAR(255);
       UPDATE users SET email_address = email;
       (both v1.x blue and v1.x+1 green work against this schema)

   release 3 (v2.0, CONTRACT):
     code:  SELECT email_address FROM users
     schema migration (after cutover + verification window):
       ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN email;

   each release is reversible (router flip);
   zero downtime; cost = 2 extra releases + temp duplicated column
```

### Q3. During a blue-green cutover, green's error rate spikes from 0.1% to 5% within the first minute. What do you do?
**Answer:** The automated canary analysis should detect this immediately and roll back automatically — the router flips back to 100% blue within seconds, users see a brief blip, and blue continues serving. If the automation did not catch it (threshold too loose, metrics lagging), the on-call engineer should manually trigger the rollback: flip the router to 100% blue, confirm green is receiving zero traffic, and verify blue's error rate returns to baseline. Once stable, the incident moves into diagnosis: what was different about green? Common causes are a code bug that only manifests in production (different data, different config, different load), a missing environment variable or secret that was not provisioned on green, a schema mismatch (green expects a column that does not exist yet — expand step skipped), a dependency that green cannot reach (a third-party API, an internal service), or a load-induced failure (green's instances are smaller than blue's and overload under real traffic). The diagnosis happens after rollback, not during — the priority during the incident is restoring service via rollback. The post-incident review produces fixes: tighten canary thresholds, add the missing pre-deploy checks, fix the code bug, and re-deploy when ready. The lesson is that blue-green's value is precisely this — a regression is caught in seconds and reversed in seconds, versus a rolling deploy where the regression affects the whole fleet over 20 minutes and rollback takes another 20.

**Visual:**
```
   T=0    cutover: router 100% blue -> 100% green
   T=30s  green error rate: 0.1% -> 5% (spike)
   T=35s  automated canary analysis: FAIL (5% >> 1% threshold)
   T=36s  router auto-flips: 100% green -> 100% blue (rollback)
   T=40s  blue error rate back to 0.1%, service stable
        |
   diagnosis (after rollback, not during):
   - code bug only in prod?  (different data/config/load)
   - missing env var/secret on green?
   - schema mismatch? (expand step skipped)
   - dependency unreachable from green?
   - green instances too small for prod load?
        |
   post-incident review: tighten thresholds, add pre-deploy checks,
   fix code bug, redeploy when ready
```

### Q4. Your team lead wants to use blue-green for every deploy, but your service is stateful with a large in-memory cache that takes 30 minutes to warm. How do you adapt?
**Answer:** The 30-minute cache warmup is a problem because green would serve cold-cache requests (slow, possibly timing out) until the cache fills. There are three adaptations. First, "pre-warm green before cutover": after deploying green but before shifting traffic, run a script that populates green's cache by replaying recent production traffic or hitting the read APIs that fill the cache. Green receives 0% user traffic during warmup, but its cache fills from synthetic load. After warmup, the cutover is instant and green serves from a hot cache. The challenge is generating realistic warmup traffic — options are shadow traffic (mirror blue's requests to green, discard green's responses), a recorded replay of recent production traffic, or a warmed cache snapshot loaded from a shared store (Redis, S3). Second, "move the cache out of process": if the cache is in Redis or Memcached rather than in-memory, both blue and green share it, and there is no warmup — green serves from the existing cache immediately. This is the better long-term design but requires refactoring. Third, "canary slowly": shift 1% traffic to green, let its cache warm from real (low-volume) traffic, shift to 5%, let it warm further, shift to 25%, and so on — by the time green reaches 100%, its cache is warm from real traffic. This sacrifices blue-green's instant cutover but adapts to the warmup constraint. The right choice depends on the cache size and the cost of refactoring it out-of-process.

**Visual:**
```
   problem: green's in-memory cache takes 30min to warm
   cold cache = slow responses, timeouts at cutover

   option 1: pre-warm green before cutover
   deploy green (0% traffic) -> replay recent prod traffic to green
   -> green's cache fills from synthetic load (30min)
   -> cutover: green serves from hot cache, instant

   option 2: move cache out of process (long-term fix)
   blue + green both use shared Redis/Memcached
   no warmup needed, green serves from existing cache immediately
   requires refactoring but solves the problem permanently

   option 3: canary slowly (sacrifice instant cutover)
   1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%
   green's cache warms from real traffic at each stage
   by 100%, cache is warm

   recommendation: option 2 (refactor) if cache is critical path,
   option 1 (pre-warm) as short-term mitigation
```

### Q5. Your blue-green deploys work, but releases take 90 minutes end-to-end because of manual approval gates. How do you speed this up without losing safety?
**Answer:** The 90 minutes is dominated by human wait time, not execution time — engineers reviewing dashboards, waiting for approval, manually verifying. The fix is to replace manual gates with automated canary analysis, following the Spinnaker/Kayenta model. First, instrument the service with high-quality metrics: error rate, p99 latency, CPU, and at least one business KPI (conversion rate, transactions per second). Second, build automated canary analysis that compares green's metrics to blue's using statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U for distribution shifts, t-tests for mean changes) and produces a pass/fail score. Third, codify the release pipeline as code (Spinnaker pipeline, Argo Rollouts, GitHub Actions): deploy green, smoke test, 1% canary, analyze, 5%, analyze, 25%, analyze, 100% — each step automated, with rollback also automated on analysis failure. Fourth, retain human approval only for genuinely high-risk releases (schema migrations, major version upgrades) and let routine releases proceed without approval. The result: routine releases complete in 10–15 minutes (mostly the canary observation windows), with the same or better safety than the 90-minute manual process — because statistical analysis catches subtle regressions that humans miss in dashboards. The trade-off is significant upfront investment in metrics, canary analysis tooling, and pipeline codification — typically a multi-month project, but with permanent payoff.

**Visual:**
```
   BEFORE (90min, manual):
   deploy green (5m) -> manual review dashboards (20m wait)
   -> manual approval (15m wait) -> 1% canary (10m)
   -> manual review (15m wait) -> 25% (10m)
   -> manual approval (10m wait) -> 100% (5m)
   total: 90min, dominated by human wait time

   AFTER (15min, automated):
   deploy green (5m) -> smoke test (2m) -> 1% canary (3m)
   -> auto analyze (instant) -> 5% (2m) -> auto analyze
   -> 25% (2m) -> auto analyze -> 100% (1m)
   total: 15min, fully automated for routine releases

   human approval retained only for:
   - schema migrations
   - major version upgrades
   - first release of a new service
   safety: statistical analysis catches subtle regressions humans miss
```

### Q6. You are running blue-green on AWS with an ALB target group swap. After cutover, some users report being logged out. What is happening?
**Answer:** The logout symptom indicates that user session state was tied to the blue environment specifically, not shared between blue and green. The most common cause is in-memory session state on the application instances — when traffic shifts from blue to green, the session that lived in blue's memory is gone, and green sees the user as a new request without a session, so it logs them out. The fix is to move session state out of process: store sessions in Redis (or DynamoDB, or any shared store) so both blue and green read and write the same session data, and a cutover does not lose any sessions. A second cause is a cookie domain or path mismatch — if green is configured with a slightly different cookie domain (say, `app.example.com` versus `.example.com`), the browser may not send the session cookie to green, and green treats the user as logged out. The fix is to ensure blue and green use identical cookie configuration via shared configuration (not environment-specific). A third cause is a JWT signing key mismatch — if green uses a different signing key than blue, JWTs issued by blue are rejected by green, and the user is logged out. The fix is to share signing keys across environments (via a secrets manager) or to support key rotation (accept JWTs signed by either the old or new key during the transition window). The lesson is that blue-green requires shared external state — sessions, caches, signing keys — so the cutover is transparent to users.

**Visual:**
```
   symptom: users logged out after blue -> green cutover
        |
   causes:
   1. in-memory session state (blue's sessions lost on cutover)
      fix: move sessions to Redis (shared between blue + green)
        |
   2. cookie domain/path mismatch (green's cookies differ from blue's)
      fix: identical cookie config via shared configuration
        |
   3. JWT signing key mismatch (green rejects blue's JWTs)
      fix: share signing keys via secrets manager, support key rotation
        |
   lesson: blue-green requires shared external state
     - sessions -> Redis
     - caches -> Redis/Memcached
     - signing keys -> secrets manager
     - anything in-process will be lost on cutover
```

### Q7. Your startup cannot afford the 2× infrastructure cost of full blue-green. How do you get most of the safety at lower cost?
**Answer:** There are three patterns that deliver most of blue-green's safety at lower cost. First, "blue-green on demand": the green environment is provisioned only at release time via Infrastructure as Code, used for the cutover, and terminated immediately after. The 2× cost is incurred only for the duration of the release (minutes to an hour), not continuously — for weekly releases this is perhaps 1% additional monthly cost, versus 100% for continuous green. The trade-off is that green takes a few minutes to provision at release time, slightly extending the release window. Second, "rolling blue-green with small canary": keep a small green environment (10–20% of production capacity) running continuously for canary validation. Deploy the new version to green, shift 10% traffic, watch metrics, and if healthy, either scale green to 100% for the cutover (brief 2× cost) or accept a rolling in-place upgrade of the blue fleet (1× cost but slower rollback). The canary catches most regressions; the rolling upgrade handles the rest. Third, "use spot for green": blue runs on on-demand baseline (always available), green runs on spot instances during the cutover window. Spot is roughly 30% of on-demand cost, so the 2× nominal cost becomes ~1.3× actual. The trade-off is that spot can be reclaimed during the cutover window, so green must be reprovisionable quickly (Infrastructure as Code makes this tractable). For a startup, I would start with "blue-green on demand" for high-risk releases and "rolling" for routine ones, graduating to full blue-green when the business justifies the cost.

**Visual:**
```
   full blue-green:              blue 100% + green 100% = 2.0x (continuous)
        |
   cheaper alternatives:
   1. blue-green on demand:
      blue 100% (continuous)
      green 100% provisioned only at release, terminated after cutover
      cost: ~1.01-1.05x (only the release window)
      trade-off: green takes a few min to provision

   2. rolling blue-green with small canary:
      blue 100% + green 10-20% canary (continuous)
      after canary passes: scale green to 100% (brief 2x) OR rolling upgrade blue
      cost: ~1.1-1.2x continuous + brief 2x at cutover
      trade-off: rolling upgrade has slower rollback

   3. spot-assisted:
      blue 100% on-demand + green 100% spot
      cost: ~1.3x (spot is ~30% of on-demand)
      trade-off: spot can be reclaimed during cutover (need fast reprovision)

   startup path:
   start: blue-green on demand for risky releases + rolling for routine
   grow:  spot-assisted full blue-green
```
